headline: Middle East conflict resolution would be a positive catalyst but energy infrastructure and supply chain disruption will take time to rebuild regardless
reasoning: Haslinger notes that a swift resolution to the Middle East conflict would be a pleasant surprise for markets, but cautions that energy infrastructure has been disrupted and will take time to rebuild, supply chains are similarly impaired, and diplomatic channels have been severely damaged over the past two years. She expects these headwinds to persist and does not view a quick resolution as a base case.
quote: obviously cycles come and go. So what do you think could be a catalyst to arrest that dislocation? But of course, we're just very conscious that, you know, energy infrastructure has been disrupted and that will take time to rebuild, supply chains have been disrupted and so that will also take time to work through the system. headline: August commodity rally — soft commodities, agricultural, precious metals, and commodity-linked currencies (AUD, CAD, peso, rand) all moved together, exemplifying cross-asset trend alignment
reasoning: Haslinger describes August as a strong month for their trend-following strategy because multiple asset classes aligned simultaneously. Energy prices rallied significantly, creating flow-on effects to supply chain logistics costs and fertiliser costs, lifting soft and agricultural commodities. Precious metals also responded, rates moved higher, and commodity-linked currencies including the Australian dollar, Canadian dollar, Mexican peso and South African rand all rose in concert.
quote: August was a great example of conditions aligning for us. We had commodities broadly rallying. So soft commodities, agricultural commodities, again, not surprising because energy prices were rallying quite significantly through August. There's obviously a flow on consequence to supply chain logistics costs and fertiliser costs. So soft commodities also responded. Precious metals also responded in, in the month of August. Rates obviously were significantly higher through that month as well. And then commodity linked currencies also performed. So the Australian dollar, Canadian dollar, pesos, South African Rand, they also responded to that thematic.

headline: Caution on private credit and private markets broadly: illiquidity and pricing opacity make them a poor diversifier if equity valuations are challenged
reasoning: Haslinger warns that to the extent investors seek alternatives to property and equities, they have turned to private credit, private equity and venture capital. She flags that private credit is already front-page news due to challenges, and that private market assets are inherently illiquid with a lack of pricing transparency. In a risk-off environment where equity valuations are under pressure, these assets may not provide the diversification investors expect.
quote: private credit is very much front of the newspaper everyday at the moment with the challenges there. And of course, many of those assets in private markets are inherently illiquid and there's a lack of transparency on the pricing. So we do really encourage investors to think about portfolio composition in good market environments, those sorts of assets might well provide you with good diversification. But if we do come into a market environment where equity valuations are challenged...we really encourage people to be thinking dynamically about their portfolio and and have they really got enough diversification to withstand that potential dislocation

headline: Structurally elevated rates and sticky inflation driven by energy prices and trade wars are creating early-phase market dislocation, with equity valuations mathematically challenged in this environment
reasoning: Haslinger argues that high debt levels were manageable when rates were low, but central banks globally are now signalling rate rises to tackle sticky inflation. Critically, this inflation is not from an overheating economy but structural factors: elevated energy prices and trade wars. She believes markets are only in the early phase of digesting elevated inflation, meaning the dislocation could be prolonged. Historically and mathematically, structurally elevated rates challenge equity market valuations.
quote: we've been dealing with very high levels of debt in the system for a very long period of time. And while rates have been low, that's kept the problem at Bay. But we're now in a position where central banks are globally indicating that rates need to rise, and that's to tackle the stickiness of inflation. And it's not inflation principally caused by an overheating economy. It's inflation that's largely contributed to by structural factors such as elevated energy prices, as you just touched on, and, you know, trade wars.
